solution:
**The amount of water vapour in air is determined in terms of its humidity.**

The chapter introduces the word directly: "The presence of water vapour in the air makes it moist. The moisture in the atmosphere is called humidity."

It then names the quantity that actually measures the amount: "The mass of vapour present in a unit volume of air is called absolute humidity", generally measured in \(\text{kg/m}^{3}\). So the fuller answer is **absolute humidity** — the mass of vapour per unit volume of air. Relative humidity is a different measure: it compares the vapour actually present with the amount needed to saturate the air at that same temperature.

**If objects of equal masses are given equal heat, their final temperature will be different. This is due to difference in their specific heat capacity (specific heat).**

The chapter defines it as "The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass of an object by \(1\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is called the specific heat of that object", and reaches it from the wax experiment: "for equal rise in temperature, the three spheres have absorbed different amounts of heat... This property is called the specific heat capacity."

The relation \(Q = m \times c \times \Delta T\) makes the reason plain. With \(Q\) equal and \(m\) equal, \(\Delta T = Q/(mc)\), so the rise in temperature is inversely proportional to \(c\): the substance with the larger specific heat warms up least.

**During transformation of liquid phase to solid phase, the latent heat is given off (released) by the substance.**

The chapter states the forward direction explicitly — a solid melting "absorbs heat energy during this transition" at constant temperature, and that absorbed energy is the latent heat of fusion. Solidification is the reverse of melting, so the same energy must come back out; the substance gives off its latent heat of fusion while its temperature stays constant at the freezing point.

The chapter's own worked Example 3 uses exactly this, for the other change of state: "Heat released during conversion of steam of temperature \(97\ ^\circ\text{C}\) into water of \(97\ ^\circ\text{C}\) \(= m_{steam} \times L_{vap}\)." Condensation gives off the latent heat of vaporization in the same way that freezing gives off the latent heat of fusion.

**Other substances** behave as the chapter describes at the top of the section: "when a liquid is heated up to a certain temperature, it expands, and when cooled it contracts." Their volume rises steadily with temperature throughout.

**Water is the exception.** Reading the graph from \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\):

- From \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) the volume of the 1 kg of water **falls** — the water **contracts** as it is heated, which is the opposite of what every other liquid does.
- At \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) the curve reaches its **minimum**, so the volume is least and therefore the **density is greatest** at \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\).
- Above \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) the volume rises again and water expands normally on heating.

The chapter says the same: "If we heat water from \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) up to \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\), it contracts instead of expanding. At \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) its volume is minimum (due to contraction). If the water is heated further, it expands and its volume increases... It means that the density of water is maximum at \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\)."

**This behaviour of water is called the anomalous behaviour of water** — "The behaviour of water between its temperature from \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is called anomalous behaviour of water."

**Specific heat capacity.** "The amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass of an object by \(1\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is called the specific heat of that object." It is denoted by the letter \(c\). The chapter gives the SI unit as \(\text{J}/^\circ\text{C}\ \text{kg}\) and the CGS unit as \(\text{cal/g}\ ^\circ\text{C}\). It is the quantity that appears in \(Q = m \times c \times \Delta T\).

**The experiment (the chapter's own, fig. 5.8).**

1. Take solid spheres of **iron, copper and lead of equal mass**, a tray carrying a thick layer of wax, a large beaker and a burner.
2. Put all three spheres in boiling water in the beaker for some time, so that all three reach the same temperature, \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\).
3. Take the spheres out and put them immediately on the thick slab of wax.
4. Note how deep each sphere sinks into the wax.

**Observation.** "It can be observed that the iron sphere goes deepest into the wax. Lead sphere goes the least and copper sphere goes to intermediate depth."

**Conclusion.** A sphere that gives more heat to the wax melts more wax and sinks deeper. The three spheres had equal mass and had all been cooled through the same fall in temperature, yet they gave out different amounts of heat — "This shows that for equal rise in temperature, the three spheres have absorbed different amounts of heat." The property responsible must therefore differ from substance to substance, and that property is the specific heat capacity. Iron has the largest of the three and lead the smallest, which agrees with the chapter's table 5.9 (iron \(0.110\), copper \(0.095\), and lead — not listed there — smaller still).

**The interval chosen is \(14.5\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(15.5\ ^\circ\text{C}\)** — a rise of exactly \(1\ ^\circ\text{C}\), but a **particular** one.

The chapter's definitions carry it: "The amount of heat necessary to raise temperature of 1 g of water by \(1\ ^\circ\text{C}\) from \(14.5\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(15.5\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is called one cal heat", and the same interval defines one kcal for 1 kg of water.

**Why a particular interval is named.** Because the heat needed is not the same in every range: "If we heat 1 kg of water by \(1\ ^\circ\text{C}\) in different temperature range than \(14.5\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(15.5\ ^\circ\text{C}\), the amount of heat required will be slightly different. It is, therefore, essential to define a specific temperature range while defining the unit of heat."

In other words the specific heat of water varies slightly with temperature, so "the heat needed to warm water by one degree" is ambiguous until the degree is pinned down. Fixing the interval makes the calorie a definite, reproducible unit.

The graph is a record of temperature against time while heat is supplied steadily to ice. It has **three distinct stretches**, and the flat ones are the important part.

**AB — flat, at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) (marked "Ice + Water (Solid + liquid)").** Heat is being supplied, yet the temperature does not rise. "Line AB represents conversion of ice into water at constant temperature. When ice is heated it melts at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) and converts into water at this constant temperature. The ice absorbs heat energy during this transition and the absorption of energy continues till all the ice converts into water." That absorbed energy is the **latent heat of fusion**; it is spent on "weakening the bonds between the atoms or molecules in the solid", not on raising the temperature. \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is therefore the **melting point of ice**.

**BC — rising (marked "Water / Liquid").** All the ice has melted, so from B onwards the heat supplied does raise the temperature. "Line BC in the graph represents rise in temperature of water from \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\)." Here \(Q = m \times c \times \Delta T\) applies.

**CD — flat, at \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\) (marked "Boiling water + Vapour", "Liquid - Gaseous state").** "Thereafter, even though heat energy is supplied to water, its temperature does not rise. The heat energy is absorbed by water at this temperature and used to break the bonds between molecules of the liquid and convert the liquid into gaseous state." That is the **latent heat of vaporization**, and \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\) is the **boiling point** of water.

**What the graph teaches:** a substance absorbs heat **without any change of temperature** while it is changing state, and the two horizontal stretches are exactly the two changes of state. The chapter adds that "The values of melting point, boiling point and latent heat depend on atmospheric pressure."

In a lake in a cold region the air above cools the surface water first.

1. While the surface water is cooling **from a higher temperature down to \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\)** it contracts, so its density increases and it sinks; warmer water rises to take its place. This circulation continues until the whole body of water is at about \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\).
2. **Below \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) the anomalous behaviour takes over.** The chapter's account of Hope's apparatus states it: "When the temperature of water starts decreasing below \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\), its volume increases, and density decreases. It, therefore, moves in the upward direction." So the colder water now **stays on top** instead of sinking.
3. That surface layer goes on to \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\) and freezes, and the ice — being lighter than water — **floats as a layer on the surface** (fig. 5.7, "Aquatic animals in cold regions", labels this Ice Layer).
4. Ice is a poor conductor, so the floating layer insulates the water beneath it. The deeper water stays liquid at about \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) — in Hope's apparatus, "The temperature of water in the lower part (\(T_1\)), however, remains at \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) for some time."

**Result:** the lake freezes only from the top downwards and never solidifies right through, so fish, other aquatic animals and plants survive below the ice "even when the atmospheric temperature goes below \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\)". Had water gone on contracting below \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) like an ordinary liquid, the cold water would have kept sinking and the lake would have frozen solid from the bottom up, killing everything in it.

[Note: the chapter poses this in a "Use your brain power!" box and does not print an answer for it. The explanation above is assembled from the chapter's own account of Hope's apparatus and from fig. 5.7; the chapter does not itself state in prose that ice floats or that it insulates the water below.]

They are the **same process** — condensation of atmospheric vapour on a surface that is colder than the dew point of the surrounding air.

The chapter puts the two side by side: "Take a bottle of cold water out of a refrigerator and keep it outside for a while... Drops of water can be observed on the outer surface of bottle. In the same way, if we observe the leaves of plants/grass or window-glass of a vehicle in the early morning we see water droplets collected on the surface."

**The mechanism, in the chapter's own words:** "When air cools, due to decrease in temperature it becomes saturated with water vapour. As a result, the excess water vapour gets converted into tiny droplets."

Applied to each case:

- **The bottle.** The chilled bottle cools the thin layer of air touching it. That air is carried below its dew point temperature — "a temperature is reached at which the air becomes saturated with vapour" — and the vapour it can no longer hold condenses on the cold glass as droplets.
- **Dew.** Overnight, leaves, grass and window glass radiate heat away and become colder than the air. Air in contact with them is cooled below the same dew point, becomes saturated, and its excess vapour condenses on them as dew.

So in both, the cold body is only the trigger; the water comes out of the air, not out of the bottle or the leaf. This is also why both are evidence of vapour in the atmosphere: "Through these two observations, we sense the presence of water vapour in the atmosphere." And how readily either happens depends on how much vapour the air already holds — "The dew-point temperature is decided by the amount of vapour in the air."

Rocks are not solid throughout — they carry cracks, joints and pores, and rain or melted snow seeps into them and collects there.

In winter that trapped water cools. An ordinary liquid would keep contracting and would simply occupy less room, doing the rock no harm. Water does not: below \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\) its **volume increases** as it cools — "When the temperature of water starts decreasing below \(4\ ^\circ\text{C}\), its volume increases, and density decreases" — and it expands further still as it turns into ice at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\).

The water in the crack is confined by the rock on all sides, so this **anomalous expansion** has nowhere to go. It pushes outwards on the walls of the crack with very large force, the crack is widened, and after this is repeated over many nights the rock splits. The chapter groups the two everyday consequences together: "In cold regions in winter the pipes for water supply break and even rocks crack" — a water pipe bursts for exactly the same reason, the water inside expanding as it freezes in a container that cannot give way.

[Note: the chapter poses this as a "Use your brain power!" prompt and does not print an answer. The explanation is grounded in its own account of the anomalous behaviour of water; the chapter does not itself describe water seeping into cracks.]

**Latent heat** is the heat energy exchanged by a substance **at constant temperature** while it changes from one state to another. It is called **latent** (hidden) because it produces no change in temperature at all — a thermometer records nothing while it is being supplied or given out.

The chapter defines the two cases:

- "The heat energy absorbed at constant temperature during transformation of solid into liquid is called the **latent heat of fusion**." Per unit mass this is the specific latent heat of fusion — for ice, \(333\ \text{kJ/kg}\) or \(80\ \text{cal/g}\) in the chapter's table.
- "The heat energy absorbed at constant temperature during transformation of liquid into gas is called the **latent heat of vapourization**." For water, \(2256\ \text{kJ/kg}\) or \(540\ \text{cal/g}\).

**If latent heat is given off instead of absorbed, the change of state runs the other way:**

- A **gas condenses into a liquid**, giving out its latent heat of vaporization at the constant boiling-point temperature. The chapter's Example 3 computes precisely this: "Heat released during conversion of steam of temperature \(97\ ^\circ\text{C}\) into water of \(97\ ^\circ\text{C}\) \(= m_{steam} \times L_{vap}\)."
- A **liquid freezes into a solid**, giving out its latent heat of fusion at the constant melting-point temperature.

In short: absorbing latent heat drives solid \(\to\) liquid \(\to\) gas; giving off latent heat drives gas \(\to\) liquid \(\to\) solid. In either direction the temperature stays fixed while the change of state is going on.

The **principle of heat exchange** is used.

The chapter states it as: "Heat energy lost by the hot object = Heat energy gained by the cold object. This is called as 'Principle of heat exchange'." It holds when the two objects are isolated from their surroundings — kept "inside a heat resistant box", so "no energy can flow from inside the box or come into the box."

In practice it is applied by the **mixing method**, using a **calorimeter**: "The specific heat of an object can be measured using mixing method. For this calorimeter is used." A hot solid is dropped into water in a calorimeter and the three settle at one common temperature, giving

\(\text{Heat lost by the solid} = \text{heat gained by the water} + \text{heat gained by the calorimeter}\)

Writing each term as \(m \times c \times \Delta T\), the chapter concludes: "if the specific heat of water and the calorimeter are known, the specific heat of the solid object can be calculated."

Latent heat is what actually **carries out** a change of state, and its role is best seen in what it does **not** do: it does not change the temperature.

**During melting and boiling** the substance keeps absorbing heat while the thermometer stands still. The chapter explains where that energy goes:

- Solid to liquid: "This heat energy is utilised for weakening the bonds between the atoms or molecules in the solid and transform it into liquid phase."
- Liquid to gas: "The heat energy is absorbed by water at this temperature and used to break the bonds between molecules of the liquid and convert the liquid into gaseous state."

So the supplied energy is spent on loosening and then breaking the intermolecular bonds — on increasing the potential energy of the molecules and their separation — rather than on increasing their average kinetic energy, which is what a rise in temperature would represent. That is why the temperature-time graph is **flat** at the melting point and again at the boiling point — in fig. 5.2 these are the horizontal stretch AB at the melting point and the horizontal stretch CD at the boiling point.

**In the reverse changes** the bonds re-form, and the same energy is given out at the same constant temperature: a gas condensing releases its latent heat of vaporization and a liquid freezing releases its latent heat of fusion.

A change of state therefore cannot occur without this exchange. Until the whole of the substance has absorbed its latent heat, some of it is still in the old state — "the absorption of energy continues till all the ice converts into water" — and the temperature cannot begin to rise again.

**The basis.** Air can hold only a limited amount of vapour at a given temperature: "For a given volume of air, at a specific temperature, there is a limit on how much water vapour the air can contain." If it holds that maximum it is saturated — "When the air contains maximum possible water vapour, it is said to be saturated with vapour at that temperature" — and if it holds less, "the air is said to be unsaturated." The test is therefore **how close the vapour actually present is to that maximum**, which the chapter expresses as relative humidity: "The ratio of actual mass of vapour content in the air for a given volume and temperature to that required to make the air saturated with vapour at that temperature is called the relative humidity."

**How to determine it — two equivalent ways.**

1. **By relative humidity.** Compute

\(\% \text{ Relative humidity} = \dfrac{\text{actual mass of water vapour in a given volume}}{\text{mass of vapour needed to saturate that volume}} \times 100\)

If it works out to \(100\%\) the air is saturated; anything less means unsaturated. "The relative humidity at the dew point is 100%."

2. **By cooling the air (the dew point test).** "Suppose unsaturated air at a certain temperature is taken and its temperature is decreased, a temperature is reached at which the air becomes saturated with vapour. This temperature is called the dew point temperature." So cool the air and watch for the first appearance of droplets. If condensation begins at once — the dew point equals the present air temperature — the air was already saturated. If it has to be cooled through some interval before dew appears, it was unsaturated, and the further below the present temperature the dew point lies, the drier the air is.

The chapter's own figures show why temperature must be part of the test: air at \(40\ ^\circ\text{C}\) "can contain 49 grams of water vapour per kilogram of dry air without condensation", while at \(20\ ^\circ\text{C}\) it "can contain only 14.7 grams". The same 20 grams of vapour leaves the air unsaturated at \(40\ ^\circ\text{C}\) and supersaturated at \(20\ ^\circ\text{C}\).

**Heat is transferred from the hot object to the cold object.**

The paragraph gives the direction from the temperature changes it reports: "the temperature of the cold object goes on increasing due to gain of energy and the temperature of the hot object goes on decreasing due to loss of energy." The hot body loses energy and the cold body gains it, so the flow is hot \(\to\) cold.

The transfer does not go on indefinitely. It continues "till the temperatures of both the objects attain the same value" — that is, until the two reach a common final temperature, after which there is no further net exchange.

We learn the **principle of heat exchange** from this process.

The paragraph describes an isolated pair of objects — enclosed in a heat resistant box so "no energy can flow from inside the box or come into the box" — exchanging energy with each other and with nothing else. Because none escapes, whatever the hot object loses is exactly what the cold object gains, and that statement is the principle of heat exchange.

**Heat energy lost by the hot object = Heat energy gained by the cold object.**

The statement carries one condition, which the paragraph supplies: the two objects must be **isolated from their surroundings**, "by keeping it inside a heat resistant box (meaning that the energy exchange takes place between the two objects only), then no energy can flow from inside the box or come into the box." Without that isolation some energy would leak away to the surroundings and the two quantities would no longer be equal.

Written out with \(Q = m \times c \times \Delta T\) for each body, it becomes

\(m_{hot} \times c_{hot} \times (T_{hot} - T) = m_{cold} \times c_{cold} \times (T - T_{cold})\)

where \(T\) is the common final temperature the paragraph says both objects reach.

The **specific heat capacity** of the substance is measured using this principle.

The principle relates the heat lost by one body to the heat gained by another, and each of those is \(m \times c \times \Delta T\). The masses and the temperature changes can all be measured directly, so the only unknown left in the equation is a specific heat — which can therefore be calculated.

The chapter applies it in exactly this way, by the mixing method in a calorimeter: "Heat lost by solid object = heat gained by water in calorimeter + heat gained by the calorimeter", and "Using these equations, if the specific heat of water and the calorimeter are known, the specific heat of the solid object can be calculated."

**Given:** \(m_A = m_B = 1\ \text{g}\); the heat given to each is the same, \(Q_A = Q_B = Q\); \(\Delta T_A = 3\ ^\circ\text{C}\), \(\Delta T_B = 5\ ^\circ\text{C}\).

**Formula:** \(Q = m \times c \times \Delta T\), so \(c = \dfrac{Q}{m \times \Delta T}\).

Since \(Q\) and \(m\) are the same for both objects, the specific heat is inversely proportional to the rise in temperature. Dividing one by the other:

\(\dfrac{c_A}{c_B} = \dfrac{Q/(m \times \Delta T_A)}{Q/(m \times \Delta T_B)} = \dfrac{\Delta T_B}{\Delta T_A} = \dfrac{5}{3}\)

**Object A has the greater specific heat, by a factor of \(\dfrac{5}{3}\)** (about \(1.67\)).

The result makes sense: A took the same heat and warmed by less, so more heat is needed per degree — which is what a larger specific heat means. This agrees with the answer printed in the textbook, \(\text{A},\ 5/3\).

[Textbook note: the book prints the answer \(586.4\ \text{g}\); the correct value is \(586.5\ \text{g}\), because the final division is slightly off — \(341 \times 586.4 = 199962.4\ \text{cal}\), which is \(37.6\ \text{cal}\) short of the \(200000\ \text{cal}\) the question's own data require, whereas \(341 \times 586.51 = 200000\ \text{cal}\). The set-up in the book is right and the difference of \(0.1\ \text{g}\) does not affect the method; only the arithmetic of the last step is wrong.]

**Given:** mass of water \(= 2\ \text{kg} = 2000\ \text{g}\), to be taken from water at \(20\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to ice at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\); latent heat of vaporization of ammonia \(= 341\ \text{cal/g}\).

The item does not restate the specific heat of water or the latent heat of fusion of ice; both are taken from the chapter — table 5.9 gives water \(c = 1\ \text{cal/g}\ ^\circ\text{C}\), and Example 3 uses \(L_{melt} = 80\ \text{cal/g}\).

**Step 1 — cool the water from \(20\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\).**

\(Q_1 = m \times c \times \Delta T = 2000 \times 1 \times 20 = 40000\ \text{cal}\)

**Step 2 — freeze the water at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\).** The latent heat of fusion must be taken out of it:

\(Q_2 = m \times L_{fusion} = 2000 \times 80 = 160000\ \text{cal}\)

**Total heat to be removed:**

\(Q = Q_1 + Q_2 = 40000 + 160000 = 200000\ \text{cal}\)

**Step 3 — this heat is what the evaporating ammonia absorbs.** If \(m_{am}\) grams evaporate,

\(m_{am} \times L_{vap(ammonia)} = 200000\)

\(m_{am} = \dfrac{200000}{341} = 586.51\ \text{g}\)

**About \(586.5\ \text{g}\) of ammonia must be evaporated.**

This does **not** agree with the answer printed in the textbook, which gives \(586.4\ \text{g}\) — see the note at the top. The derivation above is the one to follow; the printed value is short by \(0.1\ \text{g}\).

**Given:** mass of ice \(m_{ice} = 150\ \text{g}\) at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\); steam at \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\), mass \(m\) to be found; final temperature \(50\ ^\circ\text{C}\); \(L_{melt} = 80\ \text{cal/g}\), \(L_{vap} = 540\ \text{cal/g}\), \(c_{water} = 1\ \text{cal/g}\ ^\circ\text{C}\). The pot is thermally insulated, so the **principle of heat exchange** applies with no loss to the surroundings.

**Heat gained by the ice** — it must first melt, then warm up to \(50\ ^\circ\text{C}\):

\(Q_{gained} = m_{ice} \times L_{melt} + m_{ice} \times c_{water} \times \Delta T\)

\(= 150 \times 80 + 150 \times 1 \times (50 - 0)\)

\(= 12000 + 7500 = 19500\ \text{cal}\)

**Heat given out by the steam** — it must first condense at \(100\ ^\circ\text{C}\), then the resulting water must cool to \(50\ ^\circ\text{C}\):

\(Q_{lost} = m \times L_{vap} + m \times c_{water} \times \Delta T\)

\(= m \times 540 + m \times 1 \times (100 - 50)\)

\(= 540m + 50m = 590m\ \text{cal}\)

**By the principle of heat exchange,** heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body:

\(590m = 19500\)

\(m = \dfrac{19500}{590} = 33.05\ \text{g}\)

**About \(33\ \text{g}\) of steam has to be mixed**, which agrees with the answer printed in the textbook.

Notice how little steam is needed for so much ice — \(33\ \text{g}\) of steam melts and warms \(150\ \text{g}\) of ice — because the latent heat of vaporization \((540\ \text{cal/g})\) is nearly seven times the latent heat of fusion \((80\ \text{cal/g})\).

**Given:** calorimeter \(m_1 = 100\ \text{g}\), \(c_1 = 0.1\ \text{kcal/kg}\ ^\circ\text{C}\); liquid \(m_2 = 250\ \text{g}\), \(c_2 = 0.4\ \text{kcal/kg}\ ^\circ\text{C}\); both at \(30\ ^\circ\text{C}\). Ice \(m_3 = 10\ \text{g}\) at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\). Let the final temperature be \(T\).

**Units first.** \(1\ \text{kcal} = 1000\ \text{cal}\) and \(1\ \text{kg} = 1000\ \text{g}\), so a specific heat in \(\text{kcal/kg}\ ^\circ\text{C}\) has the **same number** in \(\text{cal/g}\ ^\circ\text{C}\). Working in cal and g: \(c_1 = 0.1\), \(c_2 = 0.4\ \text{cal/g}\ ^\circ\text{C}\).

As in Q9(b), the item does not restate \(L_{melt}\) or \(c_{water}\); the chapter supplies them — \(L_{melt} = 80\ \text{cal/g}\) (Example 3) and \(c_{water} = 1\ \text{cal/g}\ ^\circ\text{C}\) (table 5.9).

**Heat lost by the calorimeter and the liquid,** cooling from \(30\ ^\circ\text{C}\) to \(T\):

\(Q_{lost} = (m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2)(30 - T)\)

\(= (100 \times 0.1 + 250 \times 0.4)(30 - T)\)

\(= (10 + 100)(30 - T) = 110(30 - T)\)

**Heat gained by the ice** — it melts at \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\), then the melt-water warms to \(T\):

\(Q_{gained} = m_3 L_{melt} + m_3 c_{water} T = 10 \times 80 + 10 \times 1 \times T = 800 + 10T\)

**By the principle of heat exchange:**

\(110(30 - T) = 800 + 10T\)

\(3300 - 110T = 800 + 10T\)

\(3300 - 800 = 10T + 110T\)

\(2500 = 120T\)

\(T = \dfrac{2500}{120} = 20.83\ ^\circ\text{C}\)

**The temperature of the mixture will be about \(20.8\ ^\circ\text{C}\)**, which agrees with the answer printed in the textbook.

The result is above \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\), which confirms the assumption that all \(10\ \text{g}\) of the ice does melt — had the answer come out at or below \(0\ ^\circ\text{C}\), only part of the ice would have melted and the working would have had to be redone.
